title: The kirpan and the law
hook: many countries' laws make space for the kirpan

segments.voice: Yesterday, styles of turban: the pagg, the patka, the keski, the tall dumalla. Your line was many styles, one crown. Which style caught your eye? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

A security line. Trays, belts, keys, the beep of the scanner. A man in a turban steps up and says quietly to the officer that he is wearing a kirpan, a small curved blade, sheathed, under his shirt on a cloth strap. The officer pauses. There's a rulebook somewhere for this moment, and both of them are hoping the other one knows it. Moments like that happen at school gates, courthouse doors, office lobbies and arenas. Today is about what happens when an article of faith meets a rule written for everyone.
screen: `A SECURITY LINE.` → `I'M WEARING A KIRPAN.` → `FAITH MEETS A RULE FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Start with the faith side. The kirpan is one of the five Ks, the articles the Sikh code asks the initiated to keep on the body. It is usually worn in a sheath, on a cloth strap across the body, often under the clothes. Sikhs speak of it as a sign of the duty to protect the weak and stand against injustice, and as a reminder, not a tool for a quarrel. An initiated Sikh doesn't take it off for convenience; it is part of who they have promised to be. Now the law side. Laws about blades are written to keep people safe, and they usually don't have a kirpan in mind. So when the two meet, someone has to work out how both can be honored. Laws in a number of places make space for the kirpan, and the ways they do it vary. Some laws name religious articles directly. In some places the kirpan is allowed with conditions, such as its size, a sheath, or wearing it under clothing. Some places, such as aircraft cabins, often still say no, and Sikhs find other ways, sometimes with a small symbolic kirpan. Courts in more than one country have weighed these questions, and the answers change as laws change. What doesn't change is the shape of the problem. A Sikh is asking: may I keep my promise here? The law is asking: can everyone here be safe? A good rule tries to answer yes to both. Faith and law.
screen: `ONE OF THE FIVE KS.` · `A SIGN OF PROTECTION, NOT A QUARREL.` · `ALLOWED, WITH CONDITIONS.` · `MAY I KEEP MY PROMISE? IS EVERYONE SAFE?` · then, large: `FAITH AND LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn your country's rule. You can look it up after the bell; for now, settle, and breathe. Hold the question gently. Where you live, what might the rule be for a kirpan at a school, a courthouse, an airport? Notice what you assume, and how sure you feel. Then picture both people in that security line, the Sikh and the officer, each trying to do the right thing. Wish them both a good answer. Stay with that picture until the bell. The bell holds the time.
The kirpan and the law. An article of faith worn by initiated Sikhs, and the laws in many countries that make space for it, often with conditions. Today's word.
screen: `THE KIRPAN AND THE LAW — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: faith and law. Today, look up the rule where you live, and notice how it tries to honor both safety and faith. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

original.note: Punjabi: the small sheathed blade, one of the five Ks.

trapdoor: what you thought: a kirpan is a knife, and knives are banned.
what it means: it is an article of faith, and many countries' laws make space for it.
what a scholar hears: the space usually comes with conditions, and courts and laws keep revising where the line falls.
